title: How Daylight Saving Time Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain daylight saving time: the Methuselah-style trust of Benjamin Franklin, Franklin's satirical proposal while in France, the spring forward/fall back rule set by the Energy Policy Act of 2005, and global adoption including the EU and countries that don't observe it. They trace the history from George Vernon Hudson and William Willett's lobbying through German and British adoption in World War One, US wartime use in World War Two, the Uniform Time Act of 1966, the 1973 oil embargo extension, and the 1986 golf-lobby-linked change under Reagan. They cover the energy-savings debate, farmer opposition, traffic, crime and health arguments (heart attacks, bipolar suicides, circadian rhythm), and quirky incidents such as Amtrak schedule problems. The episode closes with a contest announcement and a correction about patent trolls.

segments.title: Opening banter and Franklin's Methuselah trust
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh open with banter, then describe Benjamin Franklin's bequests to Boston and Philadelphia that were meant to grow in compound-interest trusts, and how the payout came in below his projection.

segments.title: Franklin's satire and the name of daylight saving
segments.summary: Franklin, while ambassador to France, satirically proposed waking Parisians early with cannons. The hosts say it was dismissed as satire and not a real idea, though later proposals came about a century later. They note the name is saving, not savings.

segments.title: Spring forward, fall back and current US rules
segments.summary: The hosts explain the mnemonic 'spring forward, fall back' and state the US rule: second Sunday in March to start and first Sunday in November to end, set by the Energy Policy Act of 2005. They note that the Southern Hemisphere runs the opposite seasonal schedule.

segments.title: Exemptions and global adoption
segments.summary: Arizona, Hawaii and Guam can opt out. Indiana's history of county-by-county adoption is mentioned. Estimates of countries observing DST range from 70 to 76 as of 2008. Japan, India and China are described as major industrialized nations that do not observe it. The EU standardized its schedule from the last Sunday in March to the last Sunday in October.

segments.title: Origins: Hudson, Willett and World War One
segments.summary: George Vernon Hudson, a New Zealand entomologist and astronomer, is described as an early proposer. William Willett of England, an avid golfer, lobbied Parliament, which rejected the idea in 1908; he died in 1915. Germany was the first country to adopt DST during World War One, and Britain and many other nations followed to save coal.

segments.title: World War Two, farmers and the Uniform Time Act
segments.summary: After World War One many countries dropped DST. In World War Two, 52 nations adopted it. The US kept year-round DST for three years, and Roosevelt called it wartime time. Farmers opposed it, calling it God's time. After the war, states chose individually until the Uniform Time Act of 1966 set guidelines for states that observed it.

segments.title: 1973 oil embargo and 1986 extension
segments.summary: During the 1973 Arab oil embargo the US extended DST into winter, claimed savings of about ten thousand barrels of oil a day, a figure the hosts question. In 1986 under Reagan the start moved to the first Sunday in April, adding a month, which the hosts link to golf-industry lobbying.

segments.title: Energy, economics and the arguments for and against
segments.summary: The hosts explain the theory that shifting the clock spreads evening electrical demand, and that people get outdoors and spend money. Studies found roughly a one percent energy saving. A 2001 California study with a two-hour shift found about 0.03 percent savings. Arguments about traffic, crime, and parental concerns about children at bus stops are discussed. A 2006 Indiana study by Matthew Kotchen found a one percent rise in energy use and about nine million dollars in cost.

segments.title: Health effects, Amtrak and closing thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts discuss circadian disruption, a Swedish heart-attack study showing about a five percent rise in heart attacks in the first week of DST, an Australian study linking male suicide among bipolar men to the weeks before the change, a 1990s West Bank bombing story, and Amtrak schedule problems. They reflect on time as an invented number.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Brief closing remarks and website pointer.
